podcast.title: Influence on Madonna's "Cherish" (1989)
podcast.body: Madonna's song "Cherish" incorporated elements of Doo-wop, alongside 60s Sunshine Pop and girl group energy, as a "sequel to True Blue." "echoing the prior song's girl group energy with elements of Dewap and 60's Sunshine Pop."

podcast.title: Charlie Gillett's Typology
podcast.body: Identified by Charlie Gillett in "The Sound of the City" as "vocal group rock and roll," but now better known as Doo-wop, one of the five distinct styles he identified within early rock and roll. "What he calls vocal group rock and roll, but which is now better known as Dewwap."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 8: The Fat Man and Fats Domino

podcast.title: Cross-Racial Charting (1950s)
podcast.body: Doo-wop classics such as "Earth Angel" and "Why Do Fools Fall in Love" experienced black-fronted original versions charting alongside or slightly behind covers by white vocalists, illustrating a significant aspect of early cross-racial interpretation in popular music. "the duop classic, Earth Angel, was first recorded by black quartet The Penguins in 1954... However, on Billboard's pop charts, a cover by white vocalists The Crew Cuts was the bigger hit."

srcs.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

podcast.title: Isley Brothers' Genre Shift
podcast.body: The Isley Brothers transitioned into singing doo-wop songs at Ronald's insistence after the death of Vernon, influenced by their favorite act, Billy Ward and The Dominoes. Their first record with Richie Barrett, "Don't Be Jellis," was described as a standard doo-wop ballad. "If in turn, the group could stop singing gospel music and start singing duwop songs, like the Brothers' favourite act, Billy Ward and the Dominoes."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Origin of "My Boy Lollipop" Songwriter
podcast.body: Robert Spencer, the original songwriter of "My Boy Lollipop," was a member of The Cadillacs, a prominent Doo-wop group known for their hit "Speedo." "My boy Lollipop, have been bitten by Robert Spencer of the Cadillacs, the Dewock group whose biggest hit had been Speedo."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Role of Falsetto in Vocal Blend
podcast.body: While falsetto had always been an element of the doo-wop vocal blend, it was typically a minor component. Lead vocals were generally delivered in a smooth, high tenor, rarely reaching the truly high notes. Frankie Lymon's voice, not yet broken, revolutionized this by introducing a new, prominent falsetto timbre into lead vocals, influencing subsequent vocal groups. "Falsetto had, of course, always been a part of the do-wop vocal blend, but it had been a minor part up to this point."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Roy Hammond's Musical Roots
podcast.body: Roy Hammond began his musical career as a doo-wop singer in the 1950s, before evolving into a soul singer and later incorporating funk elements into his politically themed music. This genre formed a foundational part of his diverse musical background. "Roy Hammond who was a do-up singer in the 50s and a soul singer after that"

podcast.title: Standard Progression (General Music Theory)
podcast.body: Doo-wop music is widely recognized for its "standard Dewop progression," typically a 1-6-2-5 chord sequence, which is prevalent in countless songs. The Beach Boys' "The Warmth of the Sun" begins with this progression (C, A minor) before Brian Wilson masterfully deviates into more intricate harmonic structures. "We've talked before in this podcast about the standard Dewop progression, the one minus sixth minus second fifth progression that you get in about a million songs."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
